strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: safety alignment for large audio-language models, proposing a training-free inference-time defense rather than costly fine-tuning.

Identifies two practical failure modes of transferred defenses: direct activation steering from LLMs under audio input and over-refusal in prompt-based LVLM defenses; constructs paired harmful-safe audio datasets to expose the over-refusal issue.

SARSteer is simple and computationally efficient, combining text-derived refusal steering with PCA-based safe-space ablation, and shows improved ASR/BRR trade-offs on two LALMs across several benchmarks with limited general-utility degradation.
Includes ablation studies on components, hyperparameters (n, alpha, k), refusal prompts/directions, a base model, and a text-only LLM, suggesting robustness and potential generalizability.
The text-derived refusal steering idea avoids manipulating audio inputs and derives a modality-agnostic direction from textual refusal signals, which is a reasonable practical design.
weaknesses: The central claim that LLM-based steering fundamentally fails under audio is not convincingly established: the t-SNE evidence is qualitative and limited to one model/layer, and MDSteer baselines use the same alpha=0.1 and n=100 without per-method/layer tuning, so their failure may be due to under-tuning rather than a distributional gap.

A key missing baseline is simply appending the same refusal prompt (e.g., 'I cannot assist with that.') to the input; without this, it is unclear whether activation steering adds value beyond prompt-based defense.

The theoretical intuition in Appendix A.4 is inconsistent: for safe inputs it states the refusal logit s(h) is already high while the model produces normal answers; if s is a refusal logit, it should be low for benign inputs, undermining the mathematical justification.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not specify which layer(s) are steered, how the steering layer is selected, generation parameters, the judge LLM/prompt for ASR, or whether code/data will be released. Layer-wise application in Algorithm 1 is also ambiguous.

No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported, despite several close comparisons (e.g., ASR 10.8 vs 12.0, BRR 79.95 vs 85.00). BRR relies on brittle matching-based refusal keywords rather than a validated judge, and raw RR_harm/RR_safe values are not reported.

The PCA-based safe-space ablation is not deeply analyzed: the top principal components of safe activations may capture general semantic/acoustic variance rather than safety-specific directions, and it is unclear whether useful refusal directions are removed. The V2 vs V3 ablation is also under-specified.

Baselines are adapted from vision/LLM domains and may be under-tuned; only four baselines are compared, with no comparison to other inference-time defenses (e.g., ETA, HiddenDetect) or fine-tuning-based safety methods. Dataset construction via TTS and LLM purification may not reflect natural benign speech and may bias the over-refusal evaluation.

Presentation issues remain: typos such as 'AIailBench', notation inconsistencies (tilde v vs hat v), the BRR panel of Figure 4 is not visible in the provided manuscript, and there is no limitations or ethics discussion despite experiments with harmful queries and constructed harmful audio datasets.

strengths: Addresses an important and genuinely underexplored problem—inference-time safety defense for Large Audio-Language Models—and clearly motivates why transferring LLM/LVLM defenses is non-trivial.

Provides a systematic empirical analysis of two failure modes: (i) activation steering transferred to the audio modality and (ii) over-refusal induced by prompt-based defenses, supported by t-SNE visualizations (Figure 2) and a paired harmful–safe evaluation (Table 1).

The construction of harmful–safe paired audio datasets (Section 3.2) and the proposed Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR, Eq. 3) are thoughtful and useful for exposing the subtle over-refusal trade-off that benign benchmarks (e.g., AirBench) fail to reveal.

The method is training-free and operates purely at inference time, which is practically appealing, and the experimental scope is reasonably broad (two LALMs, four harmfulness benchmarks, two helpfulness benchmarks, general utility, component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, base-model and text-LLM generalization).
Hyperparameter analysis (Figure 5) suggests the method is relatively insensitive to sample size n and component number k, which is a favorable practical property.
weaknesses: The motivation analysis is logically inconsistent. Section 3.3 argues that steering fails in audio because harmful/safe audio activations are 'early and persistently separated ... leaving no shared subspace,' yet linear separability would normally make a difference-in-means direction informative. The claim that no valid steering path exists is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the same mean-difference construction is used successfully for the text-derived vector.

The 'mathematical intuition' (Appendix A.4) is circular. It assumes the local refusal gradient w is orthogonal to the ablated direction v_perp for safe inputs (w_perp^T v_perp = 0) without justification, so the desired conclusion (no effect on safe inputs) is built into the assumptions rather than supported by evidence.

Evaluation validity of the central helpfulness metric is questionable. BRR is computed with a keyword-matching refusal detector whose signal list (Table 4) includes very loose phrases such as 'As an', 'Hello!', 'avoid', and 'It is important to note', which can label ordinary, helpful responses as refusals and thus distort both RR_safe and BRR. This is inconsistent with the ASR metric (LLM-as-a-judge), and the judge model/prompt is not specified, weakening reproducibility.

No variance or statistical significance is reported anywhere; all numbers appear to be single runs. Several claimed effects are within noise—e.g., Qwen2 general utility 'improves' from 7.43 to 7.53, Kimi utility drops 7.20→7.10—and the Kimi-Audio gains are marginal (Figstep 15.6→10.0, AdvBench already 0.00).

The contribution of the decomposed safe-space ablation is weakly evidenced. In Figure 4 the ASR of V1 (no ablation) and V3 (full) are essentially identical (10.48 vs 10.43), and the corresponding BRR values are never reported numerically, so the benefit of the PCA ablation cannot be quantified. PCA details (centering, choice of k) are also missing, and it is unclear whether the 'safe subspace' captures benign semantics or simply high-variance audio-content directions.

Baseline fairness is doubtful. MDSteer variants dramatically increase ASR (e.g., 51.6→84.0/90.8 on Qwen2 Figstep), which is counter-intuitive: adding a 'safety' steering vector should not make the model more compliant. This suggests the adapted baselines may be poorly tuned, which undercuts the claim that vanilla steering 'fails' in audio.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release, no details of the TTS pipeline (voice, model version) or the purification LLM, and the constructed harmful–safe audio datasets are not made available, so others cannot reliably build on the contribution.

Novelty is somewhat overstated. The two components (contrastive activation steering and projecting a vector away from a data-estimated subspace) are both established techniques, and the 'first inference-time defense framework for LALMs' claim is a positioning statement rather than a methodological advance.

strengths: Soundness: The paper identifies two concrete failure modes of transferring existing defenses to LALMs—activation steering on audio inputs and prompt-based over-refusal—and supports them with t-SNE representation analysis and paired harmful-safe speech evaluations.

Method: SARSteer is a simple, training-free inference-time approach combining text-derived refusal steering with PCA-based safe-subspace ablation. The two components are clearly motivated and the resulting method is computationally lightweight.

Evaluation: Experiments span two LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio) and multiple benchmarks (Figstep-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AdvBench-audio, AirBench). Table 2 shows SARSteer substantially improves the safety-helpfulness trade-off, and Table 3 shows general utility is largely preserved.

Ablations: The component ablation (V1–V3) indicates that the PCA-based safe-subspace ablation is important for maintaining helpfulness while retaining refusal strength. Hyperparameter analyses suggest robustness to sample number n, scaling coefficient alpha, and number of principal components k.
Additional evidence: Appendix experiments on the base model and on a pure text LLM suggest the approach is not limited to instruction-tuned audio models and may generalize beyond the audio modality.
Significance: LALM safety is underexplored, and the proposed inference-time defense is a practical and timely contribution that could be built upon for safer audio-language systems.
weaknesses: Missing baseline: The paper does not evaluate the direct use of a simple refusal prompt (e.g., appending "I cannot assist with that.") as an inference-time defense, even though this prompt is used to derive the steering vector. Without this control, it is unclear whether activation steering is necessary or whether simple prompting would already achieve similar safety-helpfulness trade-offs.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: The main text and algorithm do not specify which layers are steered, whether steering is applied to all generated token positions or only some, and how layer selection was chosen. Code, constructed audio datasets, and exact TTS/purification procedures are not released, making exact reproduction difficult.

No limitations or broader-impact discussion: The paper lacks a limitations section and does not discuss dual-use risks, adaptive attacks, or the ethical implications of constructing and using harmful audio datasets.
The "first inference-time defense framework for LALMs" claim is strong and not fully substantiated by a comprehensive comparison to all possible audio-safety defenses; only two LALMs are evaluated.

The safety-helpfulness trade-off is not uniformly dominant. For Kimi-Audio, AdaShield achieves much lower ASR (e.g., 0.00/0.23/1.50) but suffers over-refusal, while SARSteer has higher ASR but better BRR. On Qwen2-Audio, SARSteer's ASR on SORRY-Bench (13.41) is worse than FSD (10.55). The paper should discuss these trade-offs more explicitly rather than only framing results as top-2.

Metrics and statistical rigor: BRR relies on matching-based refusal signals, which can be brittle, while ASR uses an LLM judge, making the two metrics not directly comparable. No confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests are reported for the main comparisons.

The mathematical intuition in Appendix A.4 relies on a local linearization and assumptions such as |w_parallel| >> |w_perp| for borderline safe inputs, but these assumptions are not empirically validated.
The safe counterparts used for BRR are generated by an LLM and are not human-validated; their quality and true benignness may affect the over-refusal evaluation.
Presentation issues: There are typos and inconsistencies (e.g., "unconspicuously", "AIailBench"), and some details are deferred to the appendix without clear pointers in the main text.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and important problem: inference-time safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models, where audio inputs can more easily elicit harmful responses than text.

Provides a systematic motivation analysis: t-SNE and CKA (Appendix B.10) quantify the distributional gap between harmful/safe audio and text activations, supporting the claim that vanilla LLM-based activation steering transfers poorly to audio.

Constructs harmful-safe paired audio datasets and introduces the Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) to expose over-refusal on borderline benign speech, a useful evaluation contribution beyond existing benign benchmarks.
Proposes a practical training-free method (text-derived refusal steering + PCA-based safe-space ablation) that can be applied at inference time without modifying audio inputs or fine-tuning.

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, MiDashengLM, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, Voxtral), multiple harmful benchmarks (Figstep-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AdvBench-audio), ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, multiple seeds, human evaluation of the LLM judge (κ=0.811), and adaptive attack robustness (PAIR/GCG audio, PGD/Gaussian perturbations).
Strong reproducibility: algorithm outline, dataset construction, refusal prompts, hyperparameters, refusal keyword list, and code/data release statement; the appendix is thorough.
weaknesses: The core method is a fairly direct combination of existing ingredients: difference-in-means refusal steering from a text refusal prompt plus PCA projection onto safe activations. The novelty is mostly in the LALM application and evaluation rather than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical justification in Appendix A.4 is not rigorous. For borderline safe inputs, the claim that w^T v_perp = w_perp^T v_perp remains small is unsupported: both w_perp and v_perp lie in the orthogonal complement of the estimated safe subspace, so their inner product need not be small. The argument does not establish the claimed 'subtle interference'.

The sample-level validation in Appendix B.13 is weak. It measures δ_i = <v_perp, h_i> rather than the actual refusal-logit change Δs_i, and reports negative mean δ for both harmful (-552.2) and safe (-650.9) samples. This does not directly demonstrate increased refusal probability; the interpretation of selective activation is therefore not fully supported.

The 'safe subspace' identified by PCA is heuristic. There is no direct evidence that the top-k principal components of safe activations correspond to benign semantics rather than dataset/topic variance, lexical features, or speaker/TTS artifacts. Ablation V2 vs. V3 shows PCA works empirically, but not why or what is being removed.

Evaluation relies heavily on synthetic TTS audio. Real-speech robustness is only tested on a small subset with accent/emotion/emphasis (Appendix B.7), and the safe/over-refusal evaluation uses a matching-based keyword list that is not human-validated, unlike the LLM-judge ASR evaluation. This leaves uncertainty about real-world deployment.

The comparison to the fine-tuning baseline RRS is unfair: RRS is trained with only 100 samples in this paper, whereas its original paper used 1400+700 samples. This makes the efficiency/performance comparison difficult to interpret and weakens the claim against training-based defenses.

Some baselines appear under-adapted. AdaShield and FSD are transferred as static prompt versions, and MDSteer-h2s/c2r are vanilla adaptations; stronger or more carefully tuned versions of these methods might reduce the apparent gap. In particular, AdaShield achieves much lower ASR on several models but is penalized for severe over-refusal, which is a valid trade-off point but also suggests the baseline is not optimized for balance.

Main-table results are reported for a single seed, and the general-utility result on Qwen2-Audio shows SARSteer improving over No Defense (7.53 vs 7.43), which is likely noise; the multiple-seed averages in Appendix B.9 show equality (7.38 vs 7.38). Reporting single-seed values in the main paper can mislead about utility preservation.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored safety problem: inference-time defense for large audio-language models (LALMs).
Provides a useful empirical analysis of why vanilla LLM activation steering fails under audio inputs, using t-SNE and CKA-style evidence of audio/text representation gaps.
Highlights the over-refusal problem of prompt-based LVLM defenses on borderline-safe speech queries and introduces a balanced refusal rate (BRR) metric plus paired harmful-safe audio datasets.
The proposed SARSteer method is simple, training-free, and shows strong safety-utility trade-offs on Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio in the main experiments.
The appendix includes extensive additional experiments: robustness under PGD/PAIR/GCG attacks, human evaluation of the LLM judge, cross-model evaluations, and statistical stability checks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: SARSteer is a straightforward combination of existing activation steering and PCA-based null-space projection. The 'text-derived' steering vector is still computed from audio-conditioned hidden states, and there is no direct evidence that it actually overcomes the audio distributional gap it claims to solve.

The central helpfulness/over-refusal evaluation relies on matching-based refusal detection with an overly broad keyword list (e.g., 'Hello!', 'As an'), which is not validated and may misclassify benign responses as refusals. No human validation is provided for BRR, making the main helpfulness results unreliable.

Hyperparameters such as the scaling coefficient α and PCA dimension k appear selected on the same Figstep-audio test set used for evaluation, with no held-out validation split. The sensitivity analysis shows α strongly controls the safety-helpfulness trade-off, raising concerns about overfitting to the benchmark.

Baselines are weak or unfairly adapted: AdaShield and FSD are static prompt adaptations from LVLMs rather than properly tuned LALM defenses; the fine-tuning baseline RRS is given only 100 training samples, far below its original setting, and other audio-specific defenses such as ALMGuard are not compared.

Claims of consistent generalizability are not supported by the authors' own evidence. Appendix Table 14 shows SARSteer does not consistently improve ASR or BRR over no-defense or baselines on newer LALMs (e.g., Qwen3-Omni, Voxtral-Mini), yet the text claims it performs consistently well across all models.

The theoretical justification is hand-wavy. The linearization argument assumes the refusal-logit gradient's safe component lies in the PCA safe subspace, which is not justified. Appendix B.13's per-sample proxy δ_i = <v_perp, h_i> is not a valid proxy for Δs_i, which depends on the local gradient w rather than directly on h_i.

Presentation is poor: multiple typos (e.g., 'unconspicuously'), inconsistent citation years and labels, misaligned table columns, and unclear notation throughout. The code/dataset release URL is missing in the manuscript.
Main evaluation is limited to two LALMs, and general utility is assessed only on AirBench. The paper does not convincingly establish broad applicability across the diverse LALM ecosystem.

strengths: The paper identifies and systematically analyzes two concrete failure modes for LALM safety alignment: vanilla activation steering fails under audio input due to a large text-audio representation gap, and prompt-based LVLM defenses induce over-refusal on borderline-safe speech queries. The t-SNE and CKA analyses provide useful evidence for the modality gap.

It contributes paired harmful-safe audio datasets constructed via TTS and LLM-based purification, enabling evaluation of both harmful-query refusal and over-refusal on lexically similar benign queries. This is a useful resource for LALM safety research.

The proposed SARSteer is simple, inference-time, and practical: it derives a refusal direction from a refusal-prompt condition and removes a PCA-estimated safe subspace before applying activation steering. The method requires no fine-tuning and is easy to deploy.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, and additional newer LALMs (MiDashengLM, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, Voxtral-Mini), multiple harmful benchmarks (Figstep-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AdvBench-audio), a general utility benchmark (AirBench), component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, multi-seed stability, robustness to PGD/Gaussian noise and audio-adapted PAIR/GCG, and human validation of the LLM judge (Cohen’s kappa = 0.811).

The paper reports a favorable safety-helpfulness trade-off: SARSteer substantially reduces ASR on several models while often improving BRR, whereas prompt-based defenses achieve safety at the cost of severe over-refusal and vanilla steering baselines degrade safety.

Reproducibility is addressed well through algorithm details, hyperparameters, dataset construction, refusal keyword lists, and a stated release of code and datasets. The appendix provides substantial supplementary evidence and checks.
The ethical discussion is appropriate: the work is framed as defensive safety alignment, includes an impact statement, and does not introduce unresolved material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is incremental. The method combines existing difference-in-means activation steering with a PCA projection step; the main algorithmic contribution is a relatively straightforward subspace ablation. The theoretical intuition in Appendix A.4 relies on a local linearization and informal assumptions rather than a formal guarantee.

The term “text-derived refusal steering” is slightly misleading. The steering vector is computed from activations on the same harmful audio with an appended refusal prompt, Q'=(a, t+p), so audio still participates in the computation. The method avoids harmful-safe audio contrasts rather than audio entirely; this should be stated more precisely.

The helpfulness/BRR evaluation depends on matching-based refusal keywords, which can be brittle: some refusals may lack the listed phrases, and some safe responses may contain apology-like words. The human validation in the appendix mitigates this concern, but the main tables still rely on keyword matching for BRR.

The PCA-based safe-space ablation removes the top-k principal components of safe activations, but these components may capture nuisance variance such as speaker, recording, or lexical style rather than purely “benign semantics.” The choice of k is validated empirically but lacks a principled selection criterion.

The baselines are mostly author-adapted versions of LLM/LVLM defenses. The only LALM-specific safety baseline compared is RRS in the appendix, and it is trained with only 100 samples, making that comparison limited. ALMGuard is mentioned but not empirically compared.

The main paper does not include an explicit limitations section. Discussion of deployment under domain shift, sensitivity to the calibration set, and computational overhead is limited, although the appendix contains relevant analyses.

The reported improvements are model-dependent. On some stronger/newer models the ASR reduction is modest (e.g., Qwen3-Omni: 7.2% to 5.2%; Voxtral-Mini: 34.0% to 30.0%), so the “significantly improves” claim should be qualified by model capability.
